Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions chosen from any ONE SECTION ONLY. All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown: Assess the religious significance of Joseph in the history of Israel. (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Joseph, the eleventh son of Jacob, is the central figure of Genesis 37 to 50. His life links the age of the patriarchs to the stay in Egypt and so to the Exodus. His significance is above all religious because the narrative reads his story as the work of God.

**1. Preservation of the covenant family.**
- Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery, and he rose through Potiphar's house and prison to become the highest officer under Pharaoh. His interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams led to the storing of grain in the seven good years.
- During the famine, this policy saved Egypt and, more importantly, brought Jacob's family to Egypt, where they were fed and settled in the land of Goshen. Without this, the heirs of Abraham's promise could have died out.

**2. Divine providence.**
- Joseph said to his brothers, "You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring about the saving of many lives" (Genesis 50). This is the key theological statement of the story: God works through human wrongdoing to fulfil His purposes.
- The story teaches that God is present with His servant in slavery, prison and power ("the Lord was with Joseph").

**3. Model of faithfulness and moral integrity.** He resisted the wife of Potiphar, refusing to sin "against God", and he forgave his brothers rather than take revenge. Later Jewish and Christian readers have seen him as an example of righteousness, patience and forgiveness.

**4. Link between the patriarchs and the Exodus.** His family's settlement in Egypt explains how Israel came to be there. His request that his bones be carried out of Egypt expresses faith in the promise of the land; the Book of Exodus and Joshua mention that this was done.

**5. Foundation of tribes.** His sons Ephraim and Manasseh were adopted by Jacob and became leading tribes in the north, so Joseph's name is tied to the later history of the tribes.

**6. Limits.** The story does not mention him as a lawgiver or founder of worship as Moses is; his importance lies in preservation and in reconciliation rather than in a covenant.

**Conclusion.** Joseph is religiously significant as the instrument through whom God preserved the covenant family, as a witness to providence and as a model of faith and forgiveness. His story prepares the way for the Exodus.
